blocks.content: The previous two topics covered the primary key, the one column chosen to uniquely identify each row, this topic covers two related ideas, candidate keys, the other columns that could have been chosen instead, and composite keys, cases where uniqueness only holds across more than one column together.

This topic covers what makes a column a candidate for the primary key role in the first place, and walks through a concrete case, a table tracking student course enrollments, where no single column is unique on its own.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646404213-2726159.png
blocks.alt: Building on primary key, this topic covers candidate keys and composite keys

blocks.content: 1. What a Candidate Key Is

A candidate key is any column, or set of columns, that could legitimately serve as the primary key, unique across every row and never null, a table often has more than one such column, only one of which actually gets chosen as the primary key.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646406291-399043493.png
blocks.alt: A users table might have email, username, and phone all independently unique

blocks.content: 2. Choosing One Candidate as the Primary Key
blocks.text: 2. Choosing One Candidate as the Primary Key

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646408342-996136856.png
blocks.alt: One candidate is chosen as the primary key, the others remain candidate keys

blocks.content: Suppose a users table has email, username, and phone number, all three are genuinely unique across users, only one of them gets formally declared the primary key, typically the surrogate id column covered in the previous topic, the remaining candidates are still enforced as unique through a UNIQUE constraint, just not as the primary key.

3. When No Single Column Is Unique
blocks.text: 3. When No Single Column Is Unique

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646409927-429852243.png
blocks.alt: An enrollments table combines student_id and course_id together as a composite primary key

blocks.content: Suppose you track which students are enrolled in which courses, a single student_id column is not unique, since one student can enroll in many courses, a single course_id column is not unique either, since one course has many students, only the combination of both columns together uniquely identifies one specific enrollment.
Declaring a composite primary key
4. Why the Combination Works When Neither Column Alone Does
blocks.text: 4. Why the Combination Works When Neither Column Alone Does

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646411800-951675699.png
blocks.alt: student_id alone is not unique, but student_id combined with course_id is unique

blocks.content: A composite key relies on the combination of values being unique even though each individual column repeats many times, student 5 appears in many enrollment rows, course 12 appears in many enrollment rows, but the specific pair, student 5 and course 12, appears in at most one row.
5. What the Constraint Actually Blocks
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646417336-494516836.png
blocks.alt: Attempting to enroll the same student in the same course twice is rejected by the composite key

blocks.content: With a composite primary key declared, an attempt to insert a second row with the exact same student_id and course_id pair is rejected by the database directly, this is precisely the constraint you want for an enrollments table, a student genuinely should not be enrolled in the same course twice.

{"headers":["Key Type","Uniqueness Comes From"],"rows":[["Single column candidate key","One column value alone, like email or username"],["Composite key","The combination of two or more column values together"]]}

blocks.title: This is a real, common table shape
blocks.content: Any table representing a many to many relationship, students and courses, tags and articles, actors and movies, tends to need exactly this kind of composite key on the pair of foreign key columns involved.
6. The Alternative, a Surrogate Key Instead
blocks.text: 6. The Alternative, a Surrogate Key Instead

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646420603-486509555.png
blocks.alt: Adding a surrogate enrollment_id instead makes it simpler for other tables to reference this row

blocks.content: An alternative to a composite primary key is adding a dedicated surrogate column, an enrollment_id, and enforcing the student_id plus course_id combination as a separate UNIQUE constraint instead, this tends to make life easier if some other table later needs to reference a specific enrollment directly, referencing a single surrogate column is simpler than referencing a two column composite key.
7. Candidate Keys vs Composite Keys, the Distinction
blocks.text: 7. Candidate Keys vs Composite Keys, the Distinction

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784646422571-898496019.png
blocks.alt: A candidate key could be chosen as primary on its own, a composite key needs multiple columns together

blocks.content: These two ideas are related but distinct, a candidate key is about which single columns qualify to be the primary key, a composite key is specifically about needing more than one column together to achieve that same uniqueness guarantee, a table can have candidate keys, a composite key, both, or neither depending on its actual data.

blocks.title: Composite keys are not a design flaw
blocks.content: A composite primary key is a completely normal, correct design choice for a table representing a relationship between two other tables, not a sign of something being wrong with the schema.
8. Common Mistakes

["Assuming every table needs exactly one single column primary key, when some relationships genuinely need a composite key","Forgetting to enforce a UNIQUE constraint on candidate key columns that were not chosen as the primary key","Declaring a composite key with columns in an order that does not match how the table is most commonly queried","Not considering a surrogate key alternative when other tables will frequently need to reference this specific row"]
items: Assuming every table needs exactly one single column primary key, when some relationships genuinely need a composite key
Forgetting to enforce a UNIQUE constraint on candidate key columns that were not chosen as the primary key
Declaring a composite key with columns in an order that does not match how the table is most commonly queried
Not considering a surrogate key alternative when other tables will frequently need to reference this specific row

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["A candidate key is any column or set of columns that could serve as the primary key, only one gets chosen","A composite key uses more than one column together to achieve uniqueness that no single column provides alone","Enrollment style tables, representing a relationship between two other tables, are the most common case that genuinely needs a composite key","The next topic, Relationships, covers the broader categories, one to one, one to many, and many to many, that these key structures are built to represent"]
items: A candidate key is any column or set of columns that could serve as the primary key, only one gets chosen
A composite key uses more than one column together to achieve uniqueness that no single column provides alone
Enrollment style tables, representing a relationship between two other tables, are the most common case that genuinely needs a composite key
The next topic, Relationships, covers the broader categories, one to one, one to many, and many to many, that these key structures are built to represent
